module.title: Unit 9: Food & Drink: Countable / Uncountable & Some / Any
module.objective: Talk about food and drinks, make polite requests and offers, and use 'must/mustn't' and 'can' to express obligation and permission.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: At the Restaurant – Ordering Food & Following the Rules
subModules.grammarFocus: Countable / Uncountable Nouns with Some / Any; Must / Mustn't & Can
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Food and drink items, restaurant vocabulary, polite requests and offers

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a short, fun passage about a young boy named Harry who visits a cooking school restaurant. You will learn how to talk about food and drink using countable nouns (like 'an apple', 'two eggs') and uncountable nouns (like 'rice', 'water'). You will also practise using 'some' and 'any' correctly, and understand when to use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'can' in a restaurant or kitchen setting. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Countable nouns (a/an, one, two, three…) vs. uncountable nouns (no plural, no a/an). Use 'some' in affirmative sentences (I have some bread) and offers (Would you like some water?). Use 'any' in negative sentences (I don't have any milk) and questions (Do you have any cheese?). Use 'must' for rules, 'mustn't' for things that are not allowed, and 'can' to ask for permission.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Food items (steak, salad, omelette, carrot cake, tomato soup), drink items (water, juice, milk, coffee), kitchen and restaurant words (chef, plate, dessert, menu, ingredient).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand the main idea (What is the text about?). Then scan for key details like specific food words, grammar patterns with 'some/any', and rules with 'must/mustn't/can'.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about food, drink, and restaurant rules.
Identify key details including specific food and drink items mentioned in the text.
Recognize countable and uncountable nouns and how 'some' and 'any' are used with them.
Understand sentences with 'must', 'mustn't', and 'can' in context.
Use skimming and scanning strategies to answer comprehension questions confidently.

contextWarmup.prompt: You are at a restaurant. You want to ask for water politely. Which sentence is correct?
options: Can I have some water, please?
Can I have any water, please?
Must I have some water, please?
contextWarmup.explanation: We use 'Can I have…' to ask for something politely, and 'some' is used in polite requests and offers. 'Any' is for negatives and general questions. 'Must' is for rules, not for polite requests.

rules: Countable nouns are things you can count: one apple, two eggs, three plates. You can use 'a' or 'an' with singular countable nouns (a steak, an omelette).
Uncountable nouns are things you cannot count individually: water, rice, bread, milk, sugar. Do NOT say 'a water' or 'two rices'. Say 'some water' or 'a glass of water'.
Use 'some' in positive sentences (There is some milk) and in polite offers or requests (Would you like some cake? / Can I have some juice, please?).
Use 'any' in negative sentences (There isn't any sugar) and in most questions (Do you have any tomatoes?).

Use 'must' for rules and obligations: You must wash your hands before cooking. Use 'mustn't' for things that are not allowed: You mustn't eat in the kitchen. Use 'can' to ask for permission: Can I sit here?

commonTrap.trapTitle: Common Beginner Pitfall: Using 'Any' in Offers
commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners think 'any' is always used in questions. But when you OFFER something to someone, use 'some', not 'any'. This is because you expect the person to say yes!
commonTrap.wrong: Would you like any cake? (This sounds like you doubt there is cake.)
commonTrap.correct: Would you like some cake? (This is a warm, polite offer.)

sections.title: Reading Passage: Harry's Day at the Cooking School

content.passageTitle: Harry's Day at the Cooking School
content.context: Harry is ten years old and he is from New York. Today, he is visiting a cooking school for children. A chef named Maria is teaching the class. Read about Harry's experience and the rules at the cooking school.
content.text:
Harry is very excited. Today is his first day at Chef Maria's cooking school. There are ten children in the class.

"Welcome, everyone!" says Chef Maria. "Before we start, you must listen to the rules. You must wash your hands. You mustn't run in the kitchen. And you must keep your plates clean."

Chef Maria shows the menu for today. "We are going to make some tomato soup and an omelette. We also have some salad and some fresh bread."

"Do we have any eggs?" asks Harry.

"Yes, we have some eggs in the fridge," says Chef Maria. "But we don't have any cheese. Can you check if there is any milk?"

Harry looks in the fridge. "There is some milk, but there isn't any butter," he says.

"That's okay!" says Chef Maria. "Would you like some juice while we cook?"

"Yes, please! I'd like some orange juice," says Harry.

After cooking, everyone sits down to eat. The tomato soup is delicious. For dessert, Chef Maria brings some carrot cake.

"Can I have some more cake, please?" asks Harry.

"Of course!" says Chef Maria with a smile.

highlights.note: 'Some' is used with the uncountable noun 'tomato soup' in a positive sentence.
'An' is used because 'omelette' is a countable noun starting with a vowel sound.
'Any' is used in a question with the countable plural noun 'eggs'.
'Some' is used in a positive answer: 'We have some eggs.'
'Any' is used in a negative sentence: 'We don't have any cheese.'
'Must' expresses a rule or obligation: washing hands is required.
'Mustn't' means it is not allowed: running in the kitchen is forbidden.
'Can I have…' is used to ask for something politely.
'Would you like some…' is a polite offer. We use 'some' (not 'any') in offers.
A fridge is a cold box in the kitchen where you keep food fresh.
Dessert is the sweet food you eat at the end of a meal.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A boy named Harry learns to cook at a cooking school and follows the kitchen rules.
A chef named Maria opens a new restaurant in New York.
Harry goes shopping for food at the supermarket.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Harry visiting Chef Maria's cooking school. He learns the kitchen rules (must/mustn't), helps find ingredients, and enjoys the food. It is not about a restaurant opening or shopping.

detailQuestions.prompt: What must the children do before they start cooking?
options: They must sit down and eat.
detailQuestions.explanation: Chef Maria says: 'You must wash your hands.' This is one of the kitchen rules the children must follow before cooking.

detailQuestions.prompt: What food do they NOT have in the fridge?
detailQuestions.explanation: Chef Maria says 'we don't have any cheese' and Harry says 'there isn't any butter.' They DO have eggs and milk in the fridge.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Harry drink while they cook?
detailQuestions.explanation: When Chef Maria offers a drink, Harry says: 'I'd like some orange juice.' So he drinks orange juice while they cook.

detailQuestions.prompt: What do they eat for dessert?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'For dessert, Chef Maria brings some carrot cake.' Omelette and bread are part of the main meal, not dessert.

questions.question: In the passage, Chef Maria says: 'You mustn't run in the kitchen.' What does 'mustn't' mean here?
options: It is not allowed – you cannot run in the kitchen.
It is a good idea to run in the kitchen.
You can run if you want to.
questions.answer: It is not allowed – you cannot run in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' means something is forbidden or not allowed. Chef Maria is telling the children that running in the kitchen is against the rules because it is dangerous.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses 'any' correctly in a question?
options: We have any eggs in the fridge.
questions.explanation: 'Any' is used in questions to ask about something: 'Do we have any eggs?' The second option is wrong because positive sentences use 'some'. The third is wrong because polite offers use 'some', not 'any'.

questions.question: Harry says: 'There is some milk, but there isn't any butter.' Which word is an uncountable noun?
questions.explanation: Milk is an uncountable noun – you cannot say 'one milk' or 'two milks'. You say 'some milk' or 'a glass of milk'. Eggs and plates are countable nouns because you can count them: one egg, two plates.

questions.question: Chef Maria asks: 'Would you like some juice while we cook?' Why does she use 'some' instead of 'any'?
options: Because she is making a polite offer and expects a positive answer.
Because juice is a countable noun.
Because 'any' is only for positive sentences.
questions.answer: Because she is making a polite offer and expects a positive answer.
questions.explanation: When we offer something politely with 'Would you like…?', we use 'some' because we expect the person to say yes. Juice is uncountable, but that is not the reason we use 'some' here. 'Any' is for negatives and general questions, not for offers.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Can I have some more cake, please?' What is Harry doing?
options: He is politely asking for more cake.
He is telling Chef Maria a kitchen rule.
He is offering cake to Chef Maria.
questions.answer: He is politely asking for more cake.
questions.explanation: 'Can I have…please?' is a polite way to ask for something. Harry wants more carrot cake, so he is making a polite request. He is not stating a rule or offering food to someone else.

questions.question: Which group of words are ALL uncountable nouns?
questions.explanation: Milk, bread, sugar, and water are all uncountable – you cannot count them individually. You say 'some milk', 'some bread', 'some sugar', 'some water'. The other groups contain countable nouns (an egg, a plate, an apple, a carrot, an omelette, a steak).

questions.question: Complete this sentence based on the passage: 'We don't have _____ cheese.'
questions.explanation: In negative sentences, we use 'any': 'We don't have any cheese.' We use 'some' in positive sentences and offers, not in negatives. 'A' is not correct because cheese is uncountable.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Star Junior Chefs Kitchen Challenge

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation during a children's cooking competition TV show called Star Junior Chefs. Harry is a ten-year-old boy who wants to become a famous chef. He is cooking with other children and talking to the show's host, Chef Bella. Listen carefully for food and drink words, countable and uncountable nouns, and the use of some, any, must, mustn't, and can. Pay attention to how speakers ask for ingredients politely and how the host explains the rules of the competition.
learningObjectives: Identify countable and uncountable food and drink nouns in spoken English.
Recognise the correct use of 'some' and 'any' when people talk about food and drink.
Understand polite requests and offers using 'Can I have...?' and 'Would you like some...?'
Identify rules and obligations using 'must' and 'mustn't' in the context of a cooking show.

keyPhrases.note: Used to politely ask for something. 'Some' is used here because it is a polite request.
Used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences to say something is not available.
A polite way to offer food or drink to someone. We use 'some' in offers.
Used to express a rule or obligation that is very important.
Used to say something is not allowed or prohibited.

keyPhrases.meaning: Kita tidak punya telur sama sekali.
keyPhrases.note: Used with countable nouns in negative sentences. 'Any' replaces 'some' in negatives.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'can' reduces from /kæn/ to /kən/, and 'some' reduces from /sʌm/ to /səm/. The vowels become shorter and weaker.
In natural speech, 'is not' contracts to 'isn't'. The /t/ at the end of 'isn't' often becomes a glottal stop before 'any'.
In fast speech, 'would you' blends together into /wʊdʒə/. This is very common in everyday spoken English.
In connected speech, 'must not' contracts to 'mustn't'. The /t/ at the end of 'mustn't' is often silent before a vowel, linking directly to 'eat'.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Cooking Challenge in the Star Junior Chefs Kitchen

content.context: Harry is at the Star Junior Chefs TV studio. The host, Chef Bella, is explaining the rules and helping the children start cooking. Harry wants to make a special pasta dish, but he needs to find the right ingredients. His sister, Lily, is also in the competition.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between Chef Bella, Harry, and Lily during the cooking competition.

lines.speaker: Chef Bella
lines.text: Welcome to Star Junior Chefs, everyone! You must wash your hands before you start cooking.
lines.translation: Selamat datang di Star Junior Chefs, semuanya! Kalian harus mencuci tangan sebelum mulai memasak.

lines.speaker: Harry
lines.text: OK, Chef Bella! My hands are clean. Can I have some tomatoes, please?
lines.translation: Baik, Chef Bella! Tangan saya sudah bersih. Bolehkah saya minta beberapa tomat?

lines.speaker: Chef Bella
lines.text: Yes, of course! There are some tomatoes on the table. How many do you need?
lines.translation: Ya, tentu saja! Ada beberapa tomat di atas meja. Berapa banyak yang kamu butuhkan?

lines.speaker: Harry
lines.text: I need three tomatoes. And can I have some cheese too?
lines.translation: Saya butuh tiga tomat. Dan bolehkah saya minta keju juga?

lines.speaker: Chef Bella
lines.text: Sorry, Harry. There isn't any cheese today. But there is some butter and some olive oil.
lines.translation: Maaf, Harry. Tidak ada keju hari ini. Tapi ada mentega dan minyak zaitun.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Chef Bella, I want to make a cake. Are there any eggs?
lines.translation: Chef Bella, saya ingin membuat kue. Apakah ada telur?

lines.speaker: Chef Bella
lines.text: Yes, there are some eggs in the fridge. But remember, you mustn't touch the oven. I can help you with that.
lines.translation: Ya, ada beberapa telur di kulkas. Tapi ingat, kamu tidak boleh menyentuh oven. Saya bisa membantu kamu dengan itu.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Thank you! Would you like some water, Harry?
lines.translation: Terima kasih! Apakah kamu mau air, Harry?

lines.speaker: Harry
lines.text: Yes, please! Is there any orange juice?
lines.translation: Ya, mau! Apakah ada jus jeruk?

lines.speaker: Chef Bella
lines.text: There is some orange juice on the counter. You can drink it, but you must finish cooking first! Good luck, everyone!
lines.translation: Ada jus jeruk di atas meja dapur. Kalian boleh meminumnya, tapi kalian harus menyelesaikan memasak dulu! Semoga berhasil, semuanya!

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Food & Drink Orders and Rules

content.summary: In this writing lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about food and drink. You will practise using 'must' and 'mustn't' to talk about rules, 'can' to ask for permission, 'Would you like...?' to offer things politely, and 'I like / I don't like + -ing' to talk about your food preferences. Follow each step carefully and pay attention to capitalisation and punctuation.

blueprintItems.title: State a Rule with Must / Mustn't
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + must / mustn't + base verb + object.
blueprintItems.example: You must wash your hands before eating.

blueprintItems.title: Ask for Permission or Offer Politely
blueprintItems.formula: Can I + base verb + object? / Would you like + noun / infinitive?
blueprintItems.example: Can I have some water, please? / Would you like some tea?

blueprintItems.title: Express Likes and Dislikes about Food
blueprintItems.formula: I + like / don't like + verb-ing + object.
blueprintItems.example: I really like eating pizza. I don't like drinking coffee very much.

blueprintItems.title: Order Food Politely
blueprintItems.formula: I'd like + a / an / some + noun + please.
blueprintItems.example: I'd like a salad and some orange juice, please.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence needs a capital letter at the start and punctuation at the end. This makes your writing clear and correct.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'some' in positive sentences and offers. Use 'any' in negative sentences and most questions.
mechanicsRules.why: In negative sentences, we change 'some' to 'any'. But when we offer something, we use 'some': 'Would you like some cake?'

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'a' or 'an' with countable singular nouns. Do not use 'a' or 'an' with uncountable nouns.
mechanicsRules.why: Rice is uncountable, so you cannot say 'a rice'. Use 'some' instead. But you can say 'an apple' because apple is countable.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always add '-ing' to the verb after 'like' or 'don't like' when talking about activities.
mechanicsRules.why: After 'like' and 'don't like', we use the -ing form of the verb to talk about things we enjoy or do not enjoy doing.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Restaurant Rules
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: You are a restaurant manager. Write 4–6 sentences about the rules in your restaurant. Use 'must' for things people have to do and 'mustn't' for things people cannot do. Also use 'can' for things that are allowed. Remember to start each sentence with a capital letter and end with a full stop.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Welcome to my restaurant! You must sit at a table. You mustn't use your phone at the table. The chefs must wash their hands. You can ask for more water. Children must stay with their parents.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Welcome to my restaurant! You must...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: My Favourite Food & Drink
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short paragraph (4–6 sentences) about the food and drink you like and don't like. Use 'I like + -ing', 'I don't like + -ing', and 'I'd like' to order something. Use 'some' and 'any' correctly. Try to include both countable and uncountable nouns.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I really like eating pasta. I don't like drinking tea very much. I like cooking rice with vegetables. I don't have any cheese at home. I'd like some orange juice and a sandwich, please. Would you like some fruit?

practicumQuestions.prompt: You are at a café with a friend. Write 3 sentences: (1) Offer your friend something to eat or drink using 'Would you like...?', (2) Order something for yourself using 'I'd like...', and (3) Ask the waiter for permission using 'Can I...?'.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must contain three complete sentences. One sentence uses 'Would you like + some/a...?', one uses 'I'd like + a/some... please', and one uses 'Can I + base verb...?'. Correct capitalisation and punctuation are required. Use 'some' and 'a/an' correctly with countable and uncountable nouns.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Would you like some cake? I'd like a cup of tea, please. Can I have some sugar?

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 4 rules for a school cafeteria. Use 'must' for two rules and 'mustn't' for two rules. Each sentence should be about food, drink, or behaviour in the cafeteria.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must contain four complete sentences. Two sentences use 'must + base verb' and two sentences use 'mustn't + base verb'. All sentences relate to a school cafeteria. Correct capitalisation and full stops are required.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: You must wash your hands before lunch. Students must put their plates in the bin. You mustn't bring sweets to the cafeteria. You mustn't run in the cafeteria.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) about your food preferences. Include at least one sentence with 'I like + -ing', one with 'I don't like + -ing', one with 'some' or 'any', and one sentence using 'must' or 'mustn't'.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must have 4–5 sentences. It must include 'I like + -ing', 'I don't like + -ing', correct use of 'some' or 'any', and at least one sentence with 'must' or 'mustn't'. Sentences must start with capital letters and end with correct punctuation. Vocabulary should relate to food and drink.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: I like eating fruit every morning. I don't like drinking milk very much. I don't have any coffee at home, but I have some tea. We must eat healthy food every day. I'd like some fresh juice, please.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Talking About Food & Drink

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will learn how to talk about food and drink clearly and confidently. You will practise saying countable and uncountable food words, using 'some' and 'any' in spoken sentences, and politely asking for and offering food. You will also practise the correct intonation for questions like 'Would you like some tea?' and 'Do you have any milk?' Pay attention to how your voice rises at the end of yes/no questions and falls at the end of statements.
content.audioGuidance: When you say food words, speak slowly and clearly. For words with two syllables like 'pizza' or 'water', make sure you stress the first syllable: PIZ-za, WA-ter. For polite offers like 'Would you like some cake?', use a gentle rising intonation at the end. When you say 'I don't have any sugar', your voice should fall at the end because it is a statement. Practise opening your mouth wide for the /æ/ sound in 'apple' and 'carrot'.

pillars.name: Food & Drink Vocabulary Clarity
pillars.target: Pronounce common food and drink words accurately
pillars.explanation: You need to say food words like 'vegetable', 'chocolate', 'orange', and 'sandwich' clearly. Many food words have tricky sounds. For example, 'chocolate' has two syllables (CHOC-late), not three. 'Sandwich' is pronounced SAND-wich. Practise each word slowly, then say it at normal speed.

pillars.name: Some / Any in Natural Speech
pillars.target: Use 'some' and 'any' smoothly in spoken sentences
pillars.explanation: In spoken English, 'some' is often reduced to /səm/ and sounds soft and quick. We use 'some' in positive sentences and offers: 'I have some bread', 'Would you like some tea?' We use 'any' in questions and negatives: 'Do you have any eggs?', 'I don't have any rice.' Practise linking these words naturally to the next word.

pillars.name: Polite Request & Offer Intonation
pillars.target: Use correct rising and falling intonation for requests and offers
pillars.explanation: When you offer something politely, like 'Would you like some water?', your voice should rise gently at the end. When you make a statement like 'I'd like some coffee, please', your voice falls at the end. This rising and falling pattern makes you sound natural and polite in English.

pillars.name: Countable vs Uncountable Stress Patterns
pillars.target: Distinguish countable and uncountable nouns through natural stress
pillars.explanation: Countable food words often appear with 'a' or numbers: 'an apple', 'two bananas'. Uncountable food words appear with 'some': 'some rice', 'some water'. When speaking, stress the food word, not 'some' or 'a'. Say 'I'd like some RICE' and 'Can I have an APPLE?' This helps your listener understand what food you mean.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In the word 'water', the stress is on the first syllable: WA-ter. But in the compound word 'watermelon', the stress shifts to the second syllable: wa-TER-melon. Notice how the rhythm changes when the word gets longer.

The word 'chocolate' keeps its stress on the first syllable: CHOC-late. When we add 'cake' to make 'chocolate cake', both 'CHOC' and 'CAKE' receive stress. This is a compound noun pattern where both key words get emphasis.
In 'vegetable', the stress is on the first syllable: VEG-ta-ble. But in 'vegetarian', the stress moves to the third syllable: veg-e-TA-ri-an. This is a common stress shift when a word changes form.

drills.targetText: I would like some water, please.
drills.hint: Reduce 'would' to /wʊd/ and 'some' to /səm/. Stress the word 'water' and let your voice fall gently on 'please'.
Use rising intonation at the end because this is a yes/no question. Stress the word 'eggs' and pronounce the final /z/ sound clearly.

drills.targetText: There are some bananas on the table.
drills.phonetic: /ðeər ɑːr səm bəˈnɑːnəz ɒn ðə ˈteɪbəl/
drills.hint: Stress 'bananas' on the second syllable: ba-NA-nas. Link 'are' and 'some' smoothly: 'are-some'. Your voice should fall at the end.
Stress 'don't' slightly to show the negative meaning. Say 'sugar' with stress on the first syllable: SU-gar. Use falling intonation at the end.

drills.targetText: Would you like some chocolate cake?
drills.hint: Say 'chocolate' as two syllables: CHOC-late, not three. Use a warm, rising intonation at the end to make it sound like a friendly offer.

drills.targetText: Can I have an apple and some rice?
drills.phonetic: /kæn aɪ hæv ən ˈæpəl ænd səm raɪs/
drills.focus: Mixing countable and uncountable nouns in one request
drills.hint: Link 'an' and 'apple' together: 'an-apple'. Stress both 'apple' and 'rice' as the key food words. Use rising intonation at the end.

roleplay.context: You are at a small café with Mr. Khoirul. He is the waiter. You want to order some food and drinks. You need to ask what is available, order using 'some' and 'any', and politely accept or refuse offers. Use countable and uncountable nouns correctly in your orders.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Welcome to our café. What would you like to eat today?
turns.translation: Halo! Selamat datang di kafe kami. Apa yang ingin kamu makan hari ini?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Hello! I'd like some fried rice and a glass of water, please.
turns.translation: Halo! Saya ingin nasi goreng dan segelas air, tolong.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Of course! Do you want any vegetables with your fried rice?
turns.translation: Tentu saja! Apakah kamu ingin sayuran dengan nasi gorengmu?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Yes, I'd like some carrots and some tomatoes, please.
turns.translation: Ya, saya ingin beberapa wortel dan beberapa tomat, tolong.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Good choice! Would you like some dessert? We have chocolate cake and fruit salad.
turns.translation: Pilihan bagus! Apakah kamu ingin makanan penutup? Kami punya kue cokelat dan salad buah.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: I'd like some fruit salad, please. I don't want any cake today.
turns.translation: Saya ingin salad buah, tolong. Saya tidak ingin kue hari ini.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: No problem! Do you have any allergies? Is there any food you can't eat?
turns.translation: Tidak masalah! Apakah kamu punya alergi? Apakah ada makanan yang tidak bisa kamu makan?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: No, I don't have any allergies. I can eat everything. Thank you!
turns.translation: Tidak, saya tidak punya alergi. Saya bisa makan semuanya. Terima kasih!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your breakfast this morning. Talk about what food and drink you had. Use 'some' and 'any' in your story. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning! I want to hear about your breakfast today. What did you eat and drink? Please tell me your breakfast story. Use words like 'some' and 'any' when you talk about your food.
storyPoints: Tell what food you ate for breakfast (for example: some bread, some eggs, an apple)
Tell what you drank for breakfast (for example: some milk, some tea, a glass of juice)
Tell one food or drink you did not have (for example: I didn't have any coffee)
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This morning, I had some bread and two eggs for breakfast. I drank some tea with milk. I didn't have any coffee because I don't like it.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ˈmɔːrnɪŋ aɪ hæd səm bred ænd tuː eɡz fɔːr ˈbrekfəst aɪ dræŋk səm tiː wɪð mɪlk aɪ ˈdɪdənt hæv ˈeni ˈkɒfi bɪˈkɒz aɪ doʊnt laɪk ɪt/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use 'some' with the food you had and 'any' with the food you did not have. Speak slowly and clearly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using 'some' in positive sentences about food you ate, and 'any' in negative sentences about food you did not eat. It also practises common breakfast vocabulary.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about cooking a simple meal for your family. Describe what ingredients you need and what you cook. Use countable and uncountable food nouns.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, I want to hear about cooking! Imagine you are cooking dinner for your family tonight. What ingredients do you need? What do you cook? Tell me your cooking story.
storyPoints: Say what meal you want to cook (for example: I want to cook fried rice)
List the ingredients you need using 'some' and countable/uncountable nouns (for example: I need some rice, two eggs, and some oil)
Say one ingredient you don't have and need to buy (for example: I don't have any onions, so I must buy some)
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I want to cook fried rice for my family. I need some rice, two eggs, some oil, and some vegetables. I don't have any onions, so I must go to the shop and buy some.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɒnt tə kʊk fraɪd raɪs fɔːr maɪ ˈfæməli aɪ niːd səm raɪs tuː eɡz səm ɔɪl ænd səm ˈvedʒtəbəlz aɪ doʊnt hæv ˈeni ˈʌnjənz soʊ aɪ mʌst ɡoʊ tə ðə ʃɒp ænd baɪ sʌm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'some' before uncountable nouns like 'rice' and 'oil'. Use numbers or 'some' before countable plurals like 'eggs' and 'onions'. Use 'any' in the negative sentence.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises using countable nouns (eggs, onions) with numbers and uncountable nouns (rice, oil) with 'some'. It also practises 'any' in negative sentences and the verb 'must' for necessity.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a restaurant. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Order food and drinks politely using 'some', 'any', 'I'd like', and 'Can I have'. Answer his questions about your order.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to the restaurant! I am your waiter today. Are you ready to order? What would you like to eat and drink?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are sitting in a restaurant and looking at the menu. The waiter, Mr. Khoirul, comes to take your order. You want to order a main dish, a drink, and maybe a dessert. Be polite and use 'please' and 'thank you'.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly and patient waiter at a small restaurant. He speaks slowly and clearly. He will ask you what you want to eat and drink, offer you dessert, and check if you have any special requests.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'd like some chicken and rice, please. Can I have a glass of orange juice? I don't want any dessert, thank you.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪd laɪk səm ˈtʃɪkɪn ænd raɪs pliːz kæn aɪ hæv ə ɡlɑːs əv ˈɒrɪndʒ dʒuːs aɪ doʊnt wɒnt ˈeni dɪˈzɜːrt θæŋk juː/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start your order with 'I'd like some...' or 'Can I have...'. Use 'any' when you say no to something. Always say 'please' and 'thank you'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises polite food ordering using 'I'd like some' for requests, 'Can I have' for asking, and 'any' in negative responses. It builds real-world restaurant conversation skills.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a supermarket. Mr. Khoirul is the shop assistant. Ask him if the shop has certain food items. Use 'Do you have any...?' and 'Is there any...?' questions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to Fresh Market supermarket. How can I help you today? What are you looking for?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are shopping at a supermarket because you need ingredients to cook dinner. You have a shopping list but you are not sure if the shop has everything. You need to ask the shop assistant, Mr. Khoirul, about the items.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a helpful shop assistant at Fresh Market supermarket. He knows where all the food items are. He will tell you if items are available or not, and suggest alternatives if something is not in stock.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Excuse me, do you have any fresh tomatoes? I also need some butter and a bottle of milk. Is there any brown bread?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː duː juː hæv ˈeni freʃ təˈmɑːtoʊz aɪ ˈɔːlsoʊ niːd səm ˈbʌtər ænd ə ˈbɒtəl əv mɪlk ɪz ðeər ˈeni braʊn bred/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Do you have any...?' to ask about items. Use 'some' when you say what you need. Remember: 'butter', 'milk', and 'bread' are uncountable, so don't add 's'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking about food availability using 'any' in questions. It reinforces the difference between countable nouns (tomatoes) and uncountable nouns (butter, milk, bread).

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at home with Mr. Khoirul, your friend. He is visiting you. Offer him food and drinks politely. Use 'Would you like some...?' and respond to his answers.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hi! Thank you for inviting me to your home. It's very nice here! I'm a little hungry and thirsty after my long walk.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your friend Mr. Khoirul is visiting your home. He has just arrived and he is hungry and thirsty. You want to be a good host and offer him different food and drinks. You have tea, coffee, juice, biscuits, fruit, and cake at home.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is your friend visiting your home. He is polite and friendly. He will accept some offers and politely refuse others. He will also ask you questions about the food you are offering.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Welcome! Would you like some tea or coffee? I also have some biscuits and fruit. Would you like some chocolate cake?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈwelkəm wʊd juː laɪk səm tiː ɔːr ˈkɒfi aɪ ˈɔːlsoʊ hæv səm ˈbɪskɪts ænd fruːt wʊd juː laɪk səm ˈtʃɒklət keɪk/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Would you like some...?' to offer food and drinks politely. Remember to use 'some' in offers, not 'any'. Smile when you speak to sound friendly!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises making polite offers using 'Would you like some...?' with both countable and uncountable food nouns. Note that we use 'some' (not 'any') in offers because we expect the answer to be yes.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul about food rules at school. Discuss what students must and mustn't do, and what they can and can't eat or drink. Use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'can'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's talk about food rules at your school. What must students do during lunch time? What food can they eat? Are there any rules about drinks?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and Mr. Khoirul are discussing the food and drink rules at your school. Your school has rules about what students can eat, what they must do during lunch, and what they mustn't bring to school. Share these rules with Mr. Khoirul.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a teacher who is interested in learning about food rules at different schools. He will ask you questions about what is allowed and not allowed, and share his opinions about healthy eating.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At my school, we must eat lunch in the canteen. We can buy some rice and vegetables. We mustn't bring any fast food. We can drink water, but we can't drink any soda.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /æt maɪ skuːl wiː mʌst iːt lʌntʃ ɪn ðə kænˈtiːn wiː kæn baɪ səm raɪs ænd ˈvedʒtəbəlz wiː ˈmʌsənt brɪŋ ˈeni fɑːst fuːd wiː kæn drɪŋk ˈwɔːtər bʌt wiː kɑːnt drɪŋk ˈeni ˈsoʊdə/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'must' for rules you have to follow, 'mustn't' for things that are not allowed, and 'can/can't' for what is possible or permitted. Use 'any' after negative words.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay combines food vocabulary with modal verbs 'must', 'mustn't', and 'can/can't' to express rules and permissions. It also practises 'some' in positive and 'any' in negative contexts.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing each food and drink word clearly and correctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the food and drink words. Make sure each word is easy to understand.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I need some vegetables, two tomatoes, a bottle of olive oil, and some fresh bread from the bakery.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ niːd səm ˈvedʒtəbəlz tuː təˈmɑːtoʊz ə ˈbɒtəl əv ˈɒlɪv ɔɪl ænd səm freʃ bred frɒm ðə ˈbeɪkəri/
practicumQuestions.hint: Say 'vegetables' as three syllables: VEG-ta-bles. Say 'tomatoes' with stress on the second syllable: to-MA-toes. 'Olive' has two syllables: OL-ive. 'Bakery' has three syllables: BAK-er-y.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill focuses on pronouncing food vocabulary accurately. Key challenges include the silent letters and syllable stress in words like 'vegetables' (3 syllables, not 4), 'tomatoes' (stress on MA), and 'olive' (stress on OL).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences out loud. Focus on using 'some' and 'any' correctly. Pay attention to when each word is used.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise grammar in speaking. Say these sentences and focus on using 'some' and 'any' in the right places. Think about positive, negative, and question sentences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: There is some milk in the fridge. There aren't any eggs. Are there any oranges? Would you like some coffee?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðeər ɪz səm mɪlk ɪn ðə frɪdʒ ðeər ɑːrənt ˈeni eɡz ɑːr ðeər ˈeni ˈɒrɪndʒɪz wʊd juː laɪk səm ˈkɒfi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'some' in the positive sentence and the offer. Use 'any' in the negative sentence and the question. Reduce 'some' to /səm/ in natural speech. Stress 'any' slightly: /ˈeni/.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the core grammar rule: 'some' in positive statements and offers, 'any' in negatives and questions. Speaking these patterns aloud helps build automatic, natural usage in conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word pair out loud. Notice how the stressed syllable changes position between the base word and the longer word. Tap your hand on the stressed syllable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's practise syllable stress with food words. I will give you word pairs. Say both words and notice where the strong syllable moves. Tap your desk on the stressed part.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: VEG-ta-ble, veg-e-TA-ri-an. CHOC-late, choc-o-LA-tier. LEM-on, lem-on-ADE.
practicumQuestions.hint: In 'VEG-ta-ble', stress is on VEG. In 'veg-e-TA-ri-an', stress moves to TA. In 'LEM-on', stress is on LEM. In 'lem-on-ADE', stress moves to ADE. Say the stressed syllable louder and longer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill demonstrates how syllable stress shifts when food words change form. The base words (vegetable, chocolate, lemon) have early stress, but their derived forms (vegetarian, chocolatier, lemonade) shift the stress to a later syllable. Mastering this pattern improves natural rhythm.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each sentence with the correct intonation pattern. Use rising intonation (voice goes up) for yes/no questions and offers. Use falling intonation (voice goes down) for statements and 'wh-' questions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. Your voice should go UP at the end of yes/no questions and polite offers. Your voice should go DOWN at the end of statements and information questions. Listen carefully and repeat.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Would you like some tea? ↗ I'd like some rice, please. ↘ Do you have any sugar? ↗ What food do you like? ↘ Is there any bread? ↗ I don't have any milk. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wʊd juː laɪk səm tiː ↗ aɪd laɪk səm raɪs pliːz ↘ duː juː hæv ˈeni ˈʃʊɡər ↗ wɒt fuːd duː juː laɪk ↘ ɪz ðeər ˈeni bred ↗ aɪ doʊnt hæv ˈeni mɪlk ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'Would you like some tea?' let your voice rise gently at the end — this sounds warm and polite. For 'I'd like some rice, please' let your voice fall — this sounds confident. For 'What food do you like?' your voice falls because it starts with 'what'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the two main English intonation patterns essential for food conversations. Rising intonation on yes/no questions and offers (Would you like...? Do you have any...?) signals that you expect an answer. Falling intonation on statements and wh-questions (I'd like... What do you...?) signals completeness and confidence.
